summary:
Cesar department contributes no finding of its own to the record: no law, enforcement practice, incident or facility specific to this department appears in the sources available. A trans visitor to Cesar stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the more developed in Latin America.

Consensual same-sex activity has been legal nationwide since 1981 and a 2011 statute bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition with no surgical requirement, and since a rule change approved in June 2015 the sex marker on government identification is changed by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended that change, described the examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Same-sex couples have held full adoption rights since 2015, marriage equality has been available since 2016, and trans people have served openly in the armed forces since 2015. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025, and passports issued within the country have offered three gender options, male, female and X, since August 2023.

The violence picture a visitor enters is national and severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025 alone, and one report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025; a 28-second video of the assault went viral from 5 April showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands flailing in a creek unable to swim before she drowned, and her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that killings are rising.

The sharpest risk sits where armed groups operate. In Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns announced through flyers targeting "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots", gave the trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed, and threatened a further wave; in Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Reported national totals include 41 trans women killed in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime: in July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against them constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity, a pattern the UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over.
tangentialFactors:
The distance between the statutory framework and enforcement is the central turbulence. An activist quoted in a Guardian investigation of 30 July 2024 states that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording the killings of trans women as ordinary cases rather than a distinct offence; that account is not corroborated in the sources by an official statement.

An international daily's reporting of 6 August 2025 covers the wave of attacks on LGBTQ+ people across Colombia following the killing of Sara Millerey. Equaldex provides comparative context on that coverage. Neither that article nor the Guardian investigation contains information specific to Cesar, so the assessment for this department rests on the national armed-group violence and displacement baseline.

Directly relevant to document work is a 2016 report, Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS, which documented notaries refusing to process name changes and recommended ending the psychiatric pathologisation of transgender identity. Refusal at the counter therefore has a documented history even though the process no longer requires a court ruling.

A comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025, so protections that advocates expect from a single consolidated statute are not yet settled in one instrument. The Attorney General's count of 35 LGBTI murders for January to May 2025 and the count of 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 come from different compilations and are not directly comparable.
localsOnly:
Gender-marker change in Cesar is a notarial and bureaucratic process applying the national rules: no surgery and no court ruling is required, and the marker on a Colombian birth certificate may be changed since 1993, with current options F, M, NB (no binario) and T (transgénero). The Constitutional Court's ruling of 4 February 2022 ordered the government to offer the non-binary option to everyone and to ask Congress to amend the relevant laws.

On 9 July 2026 the outgoing justice minister Jorge Iván Cuervo signed Decree 0732 of 2026, which obliges public notaries to complete the request within five business days, makes the first request, including a simultaneous name change, free of charge, and shields the change history from public disclosure. Notaries in the department are bound by that decree as by the national notarial rules generally.

Residents also hold the substantive rights established nationally: legal gender recognition on self-recognition since 1993, marriage equality since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, open service in the armed forces since 2015, protection under the 2011 anti-discrimination statute, and the "trans" and "non-binary" markers on national identification documents carried since November 2025.

Residents rather than short-term visitors are the group exposed to the armed-group campaigns documented elsewhere in the country, including displacement under threat and dependence on sex work where other options are absent; the trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to relocate twice after death threats from armed men, and a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Cesar-specific source on law, enforcement practice, incidents, facilities or violence against trans people is present in the inventory, so the department's position is inferred from the national framework and from patterns documented in other departments; whether armed-group "social cleansing" activity of the Caquetá and Guajira type operates inside Cesar is unresolved and not sourced here.

Decree 0732 of 2026 carries a signature date of 9 July 2026, later than every other dated source in the inventory; its current force, any amending instrument, and the identity of the incumbent justice minister are not verified beyond that signature.

Whether the prosecutor's offices handling cases arising in Cesar record transfemicide as a distinct charge is unresolved; the only source for the contrary practice is an activist quoted in a news investigation. Likewise, whether any case from the department has been referred to the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, and whether a trans woman has been detained in the department's prisons, are not sourced; a Colombian court ruling protecting the rights of trans detainees is recorded nationally without a named court or date in the inventory.

The comprehensive trans law under legislative consideration in 2025 has no sourced outcome. Comparisons between the Attorney General's 35 LGBTI murders for January to May 2025, the count of 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025, the 41 trans women killed in 2023 and the eight killed between February and April 2024 are unresolved because the compilations differ in scope and method.
